title: In WWII prison camps, cigarettes worked as a real currency
body: R. A. Radford, an economist captured in Libya in 1942, spent the rest of the war in the Stalag VII-A camp in Bavaria and watched a complete economy grow around the Red Cross parcels. Prisoners priced everything in cigarettes, and a camp shop sold surplus clothing, toiletries and food at fixed cigarette prices; its starting capital was a loan from the Red Cross cigarette store, and **no barter was accepted**. Radford’s 1945 article in Economica recorded Gresham’s law, inflation and, especially, deflation at work behind the wire, and it became a staple of introductory economics textbooks.

slides.heading: Why cigarettes made good money
items: Everyone would accept them, smoker or not
Easy to count and to split into small amounts
Supplied by Red Cross parcels, which set the money supply

slides.prompt: What did Gresham’s law, ‘bad money drives out good’, look like in a camp paid in cigarettes?
slides.answer: Prisoners kept the better cigarettes to smoke and spent the worse ones
slides.detail: Gresham’s law says that when two kinds of money circulate at the same face value, people hoard the better and pass on the worse.

slides.heading: Boom and bust
slides.text: The money supply was the parcel supply. R. A. Radford, an economist held in the Stalag VII-A camp, recorded inflation and, especially, deflation as cigarettes flowed in with the parcels and were smoked away between them.

slides.heading: Boom and bust behind the wire

steps.label: Red Cross parcels bring cigarettes in
The money supply swells: prices rise
Cigarettes are smoked away between parcels

slides.heading: Still happening
slides.text: After smoking was banned in US prisons around 2003, the commodity money inside many of them switched to tins of mackerel fillets, exchanged for goods and services.

slides.question: Radford’s camp had a shop that sold goods for cigarettes only. What provided its starting capital?
options: A loan of Red Cross cigarettes
A grant from the Swiss embassy
slides.explanation: The shop’s capital was a loan from the bulk store of Red Cross cigarettes, and it sold goods only for cigarettes: no barter.
